title: A Young Rajah
paragraphs: The moor was hidden in mist when morning came, and the rain was still pouring down. No one could go outside. Martha was so busy that Mary had no chance to talk to her. But in the afternoon Mary asked her to come and sit with her in the nursery. Martha came with the stocking she always knitted whenever she had nothing else to do.
“What’s the matter with you?” she asked as soon as they sat down. “You look like you’ve got something to say.”
“I do. I’ve found out what the crying was,” said Mary.
Martha let her knitting fall into her lap and stared at Mary with startled eyes.
“You haven’t!” she cried. “Never!”
“I heard it in the night,” Mary went on. “I got up and went to find where it came from. It was Colin. I found him.”
Martha’s face turned red with fright.

“Eh! Miss Mary!” she said, almost crying. “You shouldn’t have done it—you shouldn’t! You’ll get me in trouble. I never told you a thing about him—but you’ll get me in trouble all the same. I’ll lose my place, and what will Mother do!”
“You won’t lose your place,” said Mary. “He was glad I came. We talked and talked, and he said he was glad I came.”

“Was he?” cried Martha. “Are you sure? You don’t know what he’s like when something upsets him. He’s a big lad to cry like a baby, but when he’s in a rage he’ll scream on purpose to frighten us. He knows we daren’t call our souls our own.”

“He wasn’t upset,” said Mary. “I asked him if I should go away, and he made me stay. He asked me questions, and I sat on a big footstool and told him about India and the robin and gardens. He wouldn’t let me go. He showed me his mother’s picture. And before I left, I sang him to sleep.”
Martha gasped with amazement.

“I can hardly believe you!” she protested. “It’s as if you’d walked straight into a lion’s den. If he’d been the way he is most times, he’d have thrown one of his tantrums and woken the whole house. He won’t let strangers look at him.”
“He let me look at him. I looked at him the whole time, and he looked at me. We stared!” said Mary.
“I don’t know what to do!” cried Martha, all in a flutter. “If Mrs. Medlock finds out, she’ll think I broke orders and told you, and I’ll be packed back home to Mother.”
“He isn’t going to tell Mrs. Medlock anything about it yet. It’s going to be a sort of secret, just at first,” said Mary firmly. “And he says everyone has to do as he wishes.”
“Aye, that’s true enough—the bad lad!” sighed Martha, wiping her forehead with her apron.
“He says Mrs. Medlock has to, too. And he wants me to come and talk to him every day. And you’re to tell me when he wants me.”
“Me!” said Martha. “I’ll lose my place—I will, for sure!”
“You can’t, if you’re doing what he wants and everyone has been ordered to obey him,” Mary argued.
“Do you mean to say,” cried Martha, her eyes wide open, “that he was nice to you!”
“I think he almost liked me,” Mary answered.
“Then you must have bewitched him!” Martha decided, drawing a long breath.

“Do you mean Magic?” asked Mary. “I’ve heard about Magic in India, but I can’t do it. I just went into his room, and I was so surprised to see him that I stood and stared. Then he turned around and stared at me. He thought I was a ghost or a dream, and I thought maybe he was. It was so strange, being there alone together in the middle of the night, not knowing anything about each other. So we began to ask each other questions. And when I asked him if I should go away, he said I mustn’t.”
“The world’s coming to an end!” gasped Martha.
“What is the matter with him?” asked Mary.

“Nobody knows for sure,” said Martha. “Mr. Craven went half out of his mind the day Colin was born. The doctors thought he’d have to be put in an asylum. It was because Mrs. Craven died, like I told you. He wouldn’t even look at the baby. He just raved and said it would be another hunchback like him, and it would be better off dead.”
“Is Colin a hunchback?” Mary asked. “He didn’t look like one.”

“Not yet,” said Martha. “But he got off to a bad start. Mother said there was enough trouble and raging in that house to set any child wrong. They were afraid his back was weak, and they’ve always been looking after it—keeping him lying down and not letting him walk. Once they made him wear a brace, but he fretted so much it made him really ill. Then a big doctor came to see him and made them take it off. He spoke quite roughly to the other doctor—though in a polite way. He said there’d been too much medicine and too much letting him have his own way.”
“I think he’s a very spoiled boy,” said Mary.

“He’s the worst young rascal that ever lived!” said Martha. “I won’t say he hasn’t been ill a good deal. He’s had coughs and colds that nearly killed him two or three times. Once he had rheumatic fever, and once he had typhoid. Eh! Mrs. Medlock got a fright then. He’d been out of his head, and she was talking to the nurse, thinking he didn’t know anything, and she said, ‘He’ll die this time for sure, and it’s the best thing for him and for everybody.’ Then she looked at him, and there he was with his big eyes open, staring at her as sensibly as she could be herself. She didn’t know what would happen, but he just stared at her and said, ‘Give me some water and stop talking.’”
“Do you think he will die?” asked Mary.

“Mother says there’s no reason a child should live if he gets no fresh air and does nothing but lie on his back reading picture-books and taking medicine. He’s weak, and he hates the bother of being taken outdoors, and he catches cold so easily that he says it makes him ill.”
Mary sat and looked at the fire.
“I wonder,” she said slowly, “if it wouldn’t do him good to go out into a garden and watch things grow. It did me good.”

“One of the worst fits he ever had,” said Martha, “was the time they took him out where the roses are by the fountain. He’d been reading in a newspaper about people getting something called ‘rose cold,’ and he began to sneeze and said he had it. Then a new gardener who didn’t know the rules walked by and looked at him with curiosity. Colin flew into a rage and said the man had looked at him because he was going to be a hunchback. He cried himself into a fever and was ill all night.”
“If he ever gets angry at me, I’ll never go and see him again,” said Mary.
“He’ll send for you if he wants you,” said Martha. “You may as well know that from the start.”
Very soon afterward a bell rang, and Martha rolled up her knitting.
“I expect the nurse wants me to stay with him a bit,” she said. “I hope he’s in a good mood.”
She was out of the room about ten minutes, and then she came back looking puzzled.

“Well, you have bewitched him,” she said. “He’s up on his sofa with his picture-books. He’s told the nurse to stay away until six o’clock. I’m to wait in the next room. The minute she was gone he called me over and said, ‘I want Mary Lennox to come and talk to me, and remember, you’re not to tell anyone.’ You’d better go as fast as you can.”
Mary was quite willing to hurry. She did not want to see Colin as much as she wanted to see Dickon. But she did want to see him very much.

A bright fire was burning on the hearth when she came into his room, and in the daylight she saw that it was a very beautiful room indeed. The rugs, the hangings, the pictures on the walls and the books had rich colors that made the room look warm and comfortable, even with the gray sky and the falling rain outside. Colin looked rather like a picture himself. He was wrapped in a velvet dressing gown and propped against a big brocaded cushion. He had a red spot on each cheek.
“Come in,” he said. “I’ve been thinking about you all morning.”
“I’ve been thinking about you as well,” Mary answered. “You can’t imagine how scared Martha is. She says Mrs. Medlock will decide she told me about you, and then Martha will be sent away.”
He frowned.
“Go and tell her to come here,” he said. “She’s in the next room.”
Mary went and brought her back. Poor Martha was shaking in her shoes. Colin was still frowning.
“Do you have to do what I wish, or don’t you?” he demanded.
“I have to do what you wish, sir,” Martha stammered, turning quite red.
“Does Medlock have to do what I wish?”
“Everybody does, sir,” said Martha.
“Well, then, if I order you to bring Miss Mary to me, how can Medlock send you away if she finds out?”
“Please don’t let her, sir,” pleaded Martha.
“I’ll send _her_ away if she dares to say a word about such a thing,” said Master Craven grandly. “She wouldn’t like that, I can tell you.”
“Thank you, sir,” said Martha, bobbing a curtsy. “I want to do my duty, sir.”
“What I want is for you to do your duty to me,” said Colin, even more grandly. “I’ll take care of you. Now go away.”
When the door closed behind Martha, Colin saw that Mistress Mary was gazing at him as if he had made her wonder about something.
“Why are you looking at me like that?” he asked. “What are you thinking about?”
“I’m thinking about two things.”
“What are they? Sit down and tell me.”

“Here’s the first one,” said Mary, sitting down on the big stool. “Once in India I saw a boy who was a Rajah. He had rubies and emeralds and diamonds stuck all over him. He spoke to his people just the way you spoke to Martha. Everyone had to do whatever he told them—that very minute. I think they’d have been killed if they hadn’t.”
“I’ll make you tell me about Rajahs soon,” he said, “but first tell me what the second thing was.”
“I was thinking,” said Mary, “how different you are from Dickon.”
“Who is Dickon?” he said. “What a strange name!”

She decided she might as well tell him. She thought she could talk about Dickon without mentioning the secret garden. She had liked hearing Martha talk about him. Besides, she longed to talk about him herself. It would seem to bring him closer.

“He’s Martha’s brother. He’s twelve years old,” she explained. “He isn’t like anyone else in the world. He can charm foxes and squirrels and birds, just the way the natives in India charm snakes. He plays a very soft tune on a pipe, and they come and listen.”
There were some big books on a table beside him, and he suddenly dragged one toward him.
“There’s a picture of a snake-charmer in this one,” he exclaimed. “Come and look at it.”
It was a beautiful book with splendid colored illustrations, and he turned to one of them.
“Can he do that?” he asked eagerly.

“He plays his pipe and they listen,” Mary explained. “But he doesn’t call it Magic. He says it’s only that he spends so much time on the moor that he knows how they live. Sometimes, he says, he feels like a bird or a rabbit himself, because he’s so fond of them. I think he asked the robin questions. They seemed to talk to each other in soft little chirps.”
Colin lay back on his cushion. His eyes grew larger and larger, and the spots on his cheeks burned.
“Tell me more about him,” he said.

“Dickon knows everything about eggs and nests,” Mary went on. “He knows where the foxes, badgers and otters have their homes, too, and he keeps those places secret so no other boys will find the holes and scare the animals. Whatever grows or lives on the moor, he knows it.”
“Does he like the moor?” said Colin. “How can he, when it’s such a great, bare, gloomy place?”

“It’s the most beautiful place,” Mary protested. “Thousands of lovely things grow on it, and thousands of little creatures are busy building nests and digging holes and burrows, chirping or singing or squeaking to each other. They’re so busy and having such fun under the earth or in the trees or the heather. It’s their world.”
“How do you know all that?” said Colin, turning on his elbow to look at her.

“I’ve never really been there at all,” said Mary, suddenly remembering. “I only drove across it in the dark. I thought it was hideous. Martha told me about it first, and then Dickon did. When Dickon talks about it, you feel as if you can see and hear everything, as if you’re standing in the heather with the sun shining and the gorse smelling like honey—and everything full of bees and butterflies.”
“You never see anything if you’re ill,” said Colin restlessly. He looked like someone listening to a new sound far away and wondering what it was.
“You can’t, if you stay in a room,” said Mary.
“I couldn’t go out on the moor,” he said in a bitter tone.
Mary was silent for a minute, and then she said something bold.
“You might—sometime.”
He moved as if he had been startled.
“Go out on the moor! How could I? I’m going to die.”
“How do you know?” said Mary, with no sympathy at all. She didn’t like the way he talked about dying. She didn’t feel very sorry for him. She felt, in fact, as if he almost boasted about it.
“Oh, I’ve heard it ever since I can remember,” he answered crossly. “They’re always whispering about it, thinking I don’t notice. They wish I would die, too.”
Mistress Mary felt very contrary. She pressed her lips together.
“If they wished it,” she said, “I wouldn’t. Who wishes you would?”

“The servants do—and Dr. Craven, of course, since he would inherit Misselthwaite and be rich instead of poor. He wouldn’t dare say it, but he always looks cheerful when I’m worse. While I had typhoid fever, his face grew quite plump. I think my father wishes it, too.”
“I don’t believe he does,” said Mary, quite stubbornly.
That made Colin turn and look at her again.
“Don’t you?” he said.
Then he lay back on his cushion and was still, as if he were thinking. There was quite a long silence. Perhaps they were both thinking strange things that children don’t usually think about.
“I like the grand doctor from London, because he made them take the iron brace off,” said Mary at last. “Did he say you were going to die?”
“No.”
“What did he say?”

“He didn’t whisper,” Colin answered. “Maybe he could tell I hate whispering. There was one thing I heard him say out loud: ‘The lad might live if he would make up his mind to it. Put him in the right frame of mind.’ He sounded as if he were angry.”

“I’ll tell you who might put you in the right frame of mind,” said Mary, thinking it over. She felt she would like this question settled one way or the other. “I believe Dickon could. He’s always talking about living things. He never talks about dead things or sick things. He’s always looking up at the sky to watch birds flying—or looking down at the earth to see something growing. He has round blue eyes, and they’re wide open from looking at everything. And he has such a big laugh with his wide mouth—and his cheeks are as red—as red as cherries.”
She pulled her stool nearer to the sofa, and her whole expression changed as she remembered his wide, curving mouth and wide-open eyes.
“Look,” she said. “Let’s not talk about dying. I don’t like it. Let’s talk about living. Let’s talk and talk about Dickon. And then we’ll look at your pictures.”

It was the best thing she could have said. Talking about Dickon meant talking about the moor and the cottage, and the fourteen people who lived in it on sixteen shillings a week—and the children who grew fat on the moor grass, like the wild ponies. It meant talking about Dickon’s mother—and the skipping-rope—and the moor with the sun on it—and the pale green points sticking up out of the black soil. It was all so full of life that Mary talked more than she ever had before—and Colin both talked and listened as he never had before. Soon they both began to laugh over nothing, the way children do when they are happy together. They laughed until they were making as much noise as two ordinary, healthy, natural ten-year-olds—instead of a hard, unloving little girl and a sickly boy who believed he was going to die.

They were having such a good time that they forgot all about the pictures and what time it was. They had been laughing out loud over Ben Weatherstaff and his robin, and Colin was sitting straight up, as though he had forgotten his weak back. Then he suddenly remembered something.
“Do you know, there’s one thing we never once thought of,” he said. “We’re cousins.”

It seemed so strange that they had talked for so long and never remembered such a simple fact that they laughed harder than ever. They were in such a mood that anything could set them off. And right in the middle of the fun, the door opened and in walked Dr. Craven and Mrs. Medlock.
Dr. Craven jumped in real alarm, and Mrs. Medlock nearly stumbled backward, because he had accidentally bumped into her.
“Good Lord!” cried poor Mrs. Medlock, her eyes almost popping out of her head. “Good Lord!”
“What is this?” said Dr. Craven, stepping forward. “What does it mean?”

Mary thought of the boy Rajah again. Colin answered as if the doctor’s alarm and Mrs. Medlock’s terror did not matter in the least. He was no more bothered or frightened than if an old cat and an old dog had wandered into the room.
“This is Mary Lennox, my cousin,” he said. “I invited her to come and talk with me. I like her. She has to come and talk with me any time I send for her.”
Dr. Craven turned to Mrs. Medlock with a look of reproach.
“Oh, sir,” she gasped. “I don’t know how it happened. There isn’t a servant on the place who would dare to talk—they all have their orders.”
“Nobody told her anything,” said Colin. “She heard me crying and found me on her own. I’m glad she came. Don’t be silly, Medlock.”
Mary saw that Dr. Craven did not look pleased, but it was quite clear that he did not dare to go against his patient. He sat down beside Colin and felt his pulse.
“I’m afraid there has been too much excitement. Excitement is not good for you, my boy,” he said.

“I would be excited if she stayed away,” answered Colin, his eyes starting to sparkle in a dangerous way. “I’m better. She makes me better. The nurse must bring her tea up with mine. We will have tea together.”
Mrs. Medlock and Dr. Craven glanced at each other, troubled, but there was clearly nothing they could do.
“He does look a little better, sir,” Mrs. Medlock ventured. “But”—thinking it over—“he looked better this morning, before she came into the room.”

“She came into my room last night and stayed a long while. She sang me a Hindustani song, and it sent me to sleep,” said Colin. “When I woke up I felt better. I was hungry for breakfast. Now I want my tea. Go and tell the nurse, Medlock.”

Dr. Craven did not stay very long. When the nurse came in, he talked to her for a few minutes, and he said a few words of warning to Colin. Colin must not talk too much. He must not forget that he was ill. He must not forget that he got tired very easily. Mary thought there seemed to be a great many unpleasant things he was never supposed to forget.
Colin looked cross and kept his strange, black-lashed eyes fixed on Dr. Craven’s face.
“I _want_ to forget it,” he said at last. “She makes me forget it. That is why I want her.”

Dr. Craven did not look happy as he left the room. He gave a puzzled glance at the little girl sitting on the large stool. She had turned into a stiff, silent child again the moment he came in, and he could not see what the attraction was. Still, the boy really did look brighter—and the doctor sighed rather heavily as he went down the corridor.

“People are always trying to make me eat when I don’t feel like it,” said Colin, as the nurse carried in the tea and put it down on the table beside the sofa. “Now, I’ll eat if you will. Those muffins look so warm and good. Tell me about Rajahs.”
